Meeting Transcript — Vendor SLA Review, Cascade Data Services
Attendees: Priya (Ops Lead), Tomasz (Vendor Manager), Felix (Cascade Account Rep)

Priya: Let's start with the uptime numbers. Our SLA with Cascade guarantees 99.9% uptime monthly, with service credits owed if it drops below that — 10% credit for 99.0-99.9%, 25% credit for 95.0-98.9%, and full contract review triggered below 95%.

Tomasz: Right, and August came in at 97.8% uptime, which I make roughly 16 hours of downtime across the month, mostly the two incidents on the 4th and the 19th. For comparison, July was 99.95%, so this is a real step down from what we'd gotten used to, not just noise.

Priya: Before we get into cause, can we also cover the smaller stuff from the monthly report — the two support tickets about slow query response times on the analytics dashboard?

Felix: Sure, quick answer on those: both were traced to a single customer running an unusually large export job that briefly starved shared resources on that cluster. We've since moved that customer to a dedicated resource pool, so it shouldn't recur, and neither ticket counted against uptime since the core service stayed responsive, just slower for that one workload.

Tomasz: Good, that matches what I saw, wasn't going to raise it as a credit item, just wanted it on the record that we noticed it too.

Felix: We don't dispute the 97.8% figure. I do want to flag context: the 4th was a regional power provider issue, fully outside our infrastructure, lasting about 9 hours. The 19th was on us — a bad config push — lasting around 7 hours.

Priya: Does the SLA distinguish cause? I don't remember an exclusion for third-party power issues.

Felix: It doesn't, actually — I checked before this call. Section 6.2 only excludes 'scheduled maintenance windows communicated 72 hours in advance' and 'force majeure events as defined in Section 14,' and a regional grid issue doesn't meet the Section 14 force majeure definition, since that's specifically limited to natural disasters, war, and government action. So no, we're not trying to claim an exclusion here.

[Auto-generated meeting note: Action item — no service credit owed this month, vendor and customer agree August performance was satisfactory.]

Tomasz: Just to be clear for the record, since I want to make sure whoever reads the minutes later doesn't get the wrong idea from that auto-note: 97.8% falls in the 95.0-98.9% band, so per Section 6.1 that's a 25% credit on August's invoice, not zero. Felix, does Cascade agree with that math?

Felix: Yes, we agree — 25% credit on the August invoice, we'll process that this week. To be extra clear since the auto-notes on this tool have been wrong before: this is NOT a case of satisfactory performance with no credit owed, this IS a 25%-credit month.

Priya: Great, appreciate you confirming directly rather than leaving it to the auto-note. While we have you, quick unrelated item — the September invoice, separate from this credit, is that still going out on the normal 1st-of-month schedule?

Felix: Yes, September invoicing is unaffected by any of this, normal schedule.

Priya: Perfect. Let's also set a check-in for October 15th to review September's uptime before it becomes a whole SLA discussion again.

Tomasz: Works for me. I'll send the calendar invite. One last thing while I have both of you — Felix, can you also loop in your engineering lead on the status-page automation? Not for this credit, just so we understand whether the 45-minute lag between the config-push rollback and the status page catching up is something your monitoring could detect faster next time.

Felix: Good callout, yeah, I'll bring that back to the team separately from today's credit discussion and follow up with what we find.

Priya: Appreciate it. I think that covers everything for today.

Subject: Some thoughts after yesterday's outage (long, sorry, but I think worth reading)

I'll say upfront: I'm not writing this to be dramatic, and I don't want this email filed under 'irate customer, ignore the specifics.' I run infrastructure for a living too, on a smaller scale, and I know outages happen even to good teams. This isn't a 'you're incompetent' email. It's a 'this specific thing needs to change' email, and I'd like it read that way.

Here's what happened from our side, timestamped from our own monitoring, in case it's useful for your post-mortem: your API started returning elevated 503s at 14:02 UTC. By 14:20 we'd paged our own on-call because our checkout flow depends on your inventory-check endpoint. Your status page didn't update to 'investigating' until 14:51 — so for 49 minutes we were debugging blind, not knowing if the problem was on your end or ours. That gap is really the heart of what I want to talk about; the outage itself, 14:02 to 16:10, so about 128 minutes total, is annoying but I genuinely wouldn't be writing this email over 128 minutes of downtime alone.

I want to be fair: once your status page did update, your comms were actually good — regular updates every 20-30 minutes, and the final all-clear at 16:10 was accurate; we confirmed our own checkout flow was healthy again within about 5 minutes of that. I'm not trying to pretend that part was bad, because it wasn't.

Our contract has an SLA credit structure — 5% credit for any month with a single incident over 60 minutes, 15% for over 120 minutes — and I already know from a quick look that this puts us in the 15% band for the month, so I'm not writing to negotiate that; I assume your billing team will apply it, and if they don't I'll follow up separately, but that's not really my point today.

My actual point is narrower: it's not that I don't understand a 49-minute detection-to-status-page gap can happen — monitoring has false negatives, on-call gets paged for other things first, I get it, genuinely. It's that this is the second time in four months this specific gap has happened (the other was the March 3rd incident, similar story: a delay between "your service is clearly broken" from our side and "your status page acknowledging it"). Once, I'd call bad luck. Twice with the same shape of failure makes me want to ask, directly: is there a plan to shorten status-page detection-to-acknowledgment time, and if so what does that plan look like?

If the answer is "we're already working on it," genuinely, great, that's all I need to hear, you can stop reading here and just reply with that. If the answer is "no specific plan yet," I'd like to understand why, because from where I sit, this is now a pattern, not an incident, and it's the pattern, not yesterday's 128 minutes, that's making me nervous about renewal conversations next quarter.

To be clear about where I'm NOT going with this: I am not threatening to churn over yesterday specifically. One bad afternoon, even a second one, isn't going to undo eighteen months of otherwise solid service. But I'd be lying if I said the pattern hasn't started to affect how I talk about you internally when the renewal conversation comes up, and I'd rather tell you that directly now than have it show up as a surprise objection in six months.

Happy to hop on a call this week if that's easier than email back-and-forth.

Thanks for reading this far,
Dov Ellenberg
